1.goal: To open on the conversation she will actually have in four months.
1.interaction: T–S, one line read out loud. No discussion here.
run: Read the subtitle with her and go on.
Do not preview the difficulty.
1.expected: Nothing to produce yet. She should arrive at the next screen knowing who she will be talking to.
1.support: If she asks what is coming, answer with the situation, not with the language: a teacher who taught the class, and no Portuguese available.
1.challenge: Ask whether she has already had a version of this conversation, and in which language.
1.monitoring: Whether the absence of Portuguese registers as the real constraint. It is the one the whole lesson turns on.
1.evidence: Nothing yet. The measurement starts on screen 3.

2.goal: To fix role, interlocutor, context and result before anything is produced.
2.interaction: T–S, reading the brief on screen together.
run: She reads the brief.
Confirm out loud: she is not his manager, and he is not obliged to accept anything she says.
2.expected: Recognition — this is the conversation the training in four months makes hers.
2.support: If the role stays vague, ask what she can do if he simply says no. The answer defines the role better than any definition.
2.challenge: Ask what a bad outcome of this conversation would look like, and what would cause it.
2.monitoring: The case is FICTIONAL and the material says so. If she wants to use a real teacher from her school, accept it — without a name, without anything identifiable.
2.evidence: How she describes a good outcome. It is the criterion the two rounds are measured against.
2.transition: Move on when she can say what a good outcome of the conversation would be.

3.goal: To see the feedback she gives TODAY, before any model. DO NOT CORRECT on this screen.
3.interaction: Role-play. You are the teacher, and you say almost nothing.
run: Sit and listen. One “right”, one “ok” — nothing more.
Let it be as long or as short as it comes out.
exact: If she stops after ten seconds, one question and nothing else: “And what would you suggest?”
3.expected: Whatever she has. Very likely: the observation stated well, and the recommendation as an instruction.
3.support: If she stops after ten seconds, ask “and what would you suggest?” — nothing more. Do not offer language.
3.challenge: None here. Anything you add contaminates the baseline this screen exists to take.
3.monitoring: Where the observation ends and the recommendation starts, and what form the recommendation takes.
3.evidence: THE RECOMMENDATION, VERBATIM. It comes back in stage 7 next to the second version, and it is what the lesson measures.
3.transition: Move on when she has given the feedback once, whole.

4.goal: To show ONE model of the same conversation — only what the task needs.
4.interaction: T–S, reading the four lines out loud, one each.
run: Read it with her, out loud, one line each.
Then the question. Do not analyze yet: the analysis is the next stage.
exact: Opening the model up, line by line: “What can he say back to that?”
If she answers “nothing”: “Then who decides what happens next?”
4.expected: She notices that the observation comes first and that the recommendation is offered rather than issued.
4.support: Ask what the teacher in the model is ABLE to say back at each point.
4.challenge: Ask which of the four lines she would find hardest to say to a real colleague.
4.monitoring: Whether she reads the model as politeness. If she does, hold the point until stage 5, where the sentences settle it.
4.evidence: The difference she names between the model and her own version — it is her own analysis before any label.
4.transition: Move on when she has named one difference from her own version.

5.goal: For her to find what makes a recommendation answerable, from the sentences themselves.
5.interaction: S sorts on screen, then T–S before the reveal.
run: She sorts the six, then Check.
Then the question, and she answers BEFORE the reveal.
5.support: The test: could he say “no, because…” and still be talking about the same thing? With 1, 3 and 5 the only answers left are yes, or a fight.
5.challenge: Ask her to rewrite number 1 so that he could refuse it without the conversation ending.
5.monitoring: The difference is NOT politeness. “Please give the instruction first” is polite and unanswerable. Make this explicit if she reaches for “being nicer”.
5.evidence: How she states the difference in her own words — it is what she will have to apply live in two rounds.
5.transition: Move on when she can state the difference in her own words.

6.goal: To put the missing repertoire in her mouth before the simulation.
6.interaction: S completes on screen, then says each line out loud to you.
run: She completes the four and says each one out loud.
Correct the FORM here — this is the stage for it.
Pronunciation: falling intonation on “might”. Rising, the suggestion turns into asking his permission, which is the opposite of the point.
6.expected: Four recommendations that say the same thing about the class, with the decision left on his side.
6.support: If the intonation keeps rising, say the same line twice yourself — once rising, once falling — and ask which one sounds like she is asking to be allowed.
6.challenge: Ask for a fifth version of her own, about the same moment, without writing it first.
6.monitoring: THIS IS WHERE THE HYPOTHESIS IS TESTED. If the forms were simply absent until now and appear immediately once given, it was repertoire, not register.
6.evidence: Whether the forms appear at once when supplied. That is the answer to the hypothesis, and it goes in the record.
6.transition: Move on when four have been said out loud, with the intonation falling on at least two.

7.goal: The whole conversation, with the repertoire available.
7.interaction: Role-play, round 1. You are the teacher, and in this round you accept and ask for detail.
run: Let her open and run the conversation.
Ask for detail with the two lines below, word for word.
Do not disagree yet. Round two is where that happens.
exact: Right — which part of the lesson was that?
And what were the others doing while that happened?
7.expected: Observation first, recommendation in a refusable form, and a close he can act on.
7.support: The three lines from the previous screen stay in view. If the recommendation comes out as an order, do NOT correct it live — note it and rebuild it in the next stage, with her sentence.
7.challenge: Ask him to be asked something: “Is there anything you would like me to look at next time?” — and see whether she can hand the turn over.
7.monitoring: Compare the recommendation here with the one you wrote down in stage 3. That comparison IS the evidence the lesson looks for.
7.evidence: The recommendation as she said it in this round, next to the one from stage 3.
7.transition: Move on when the conversation has closed on something he could act on.

8.goal: One point, and the sentence rebuilt for round two.
8.interaction: T–S, filling the board together with the two versions side by side.
run: Put her stage-3 recommendation in the third field, WORD FOR WORD, and the round-1 one next to it.
Let her see the two.
Then build the version she will use in round two.
8.expected: If the two versions differ, the lesson is visible — say so out loud. If they do not, that is data too, and it goes in the record.
8.support: If she cannot see a difference between the two, read them back to her one after the other and ask which one he could refuse.
8.challenge: Ask for the upgraded sentence with the observation attached, in one turn.
8.monitoring: The upgrade is ONE sentence. Round two is not a second lesson.
8.evidence: The two versions and the upgraded one. Together they are the record of what the lesson moved.
8.transition: Move on when the upgraded sentence has been said once.

9.goal: The same conversation with ONE new variable: he disagrees.
9.interaction: Role-play, round 2. You are the teacher, and this time you push back.
run: Same opening.
When she gets to the recommendation, disagree — using the first line below, word for word. If she holds, use the second.
He is partly right, and that is the point: he did ask a checking question, and she did not see it.
Say it with argument, never with hostility — the pressure comes from the situation, not from your tone.
exact: I did give it before they started. I said it twice, actually. They were not listening.
So you are saying it is my instruction, and I am saying it is their attention.
9.expected: She concedes the reason and keeps the observation. Something like “that is fair — and the part I would still look at is…”.
9.support: If the recommendation disappears entirely, stop and ask what she still thinks is true after what he said. That question rebuilds the turn without giving her the words.
9.challenge: Add a second objection about the two slower pairs, and see whether the concession still leaves the observation standing.
9.monitoring: Whether she concedes and holds, concedes and drops, or refuses to concede. The three are different problems and only the first is the target.
9.evidence: What survives the disagreement. It is the closing measure of the block, and it goes on the card.
9.transition: Move on when she has answered the objection and closed the conversation.

10.goal: To register the lesson and to close the block.
10.interaction: S ticks the list and answers the scale; T–S on the close of the block.
run: She reads the list and ticks what she recognizes.
Then say, out loud, that this was the last of the four — and that the next block is decided from what these four showed, not from a plan written in advance.
Say the homework out loud and never write it on the screen.
10.expected: Some of the lines ticked, one honest answer on the scale, and a date for the conversation she actually has to hold.
10.support: If she ticks nothing, read the list with her and ask which line she could use in the next conversation she already has booked.
10.challenge: Ask which of the two rounds she would rather repeat, and what she would do differently.
10.monitoring: This is the last lesson of block 1. The post-lesson record on the card feeds the lesson that closes the block, and that lesson reads the four together.
10.evidence: Her confidence reading against what round two showed. Fill the post-lesson record before you close — it is the input for the next block.
10.transition: Close the lesson, and the block.
